scale.why: Each axis is scored by the share of its own inventory the language forces. raw_d is the sum of the weights present in dimension d; W_d is the sum of every weight the inventory names there. The denominator is the inventory itself, not a chosen ceiling, so the scale needs no free constant: 100 means the language forces none of the named couplings, and 0 means it forces every one of them. The share is additive in the artifact, because a maintainer pays every forced coupling, and it is monotone, so each removed mechanism moves the score by 100 * w / sum_d W_d. There is no cap and no curve: a cap hides every mechanism above it, and a curve would price the tenth mechanism of a dimension below the first, which the inventory does not claim. Two languages that force the same severity share the same score exactly.

aggregation.label: Ranking score

core.label: Core coupling
core.why: the coupling the language's own constructs force into the code. This is primary, because once the code is written the code is what remains, and coupling is structural and cumulative.

readiness.label: Engineering readiness
readiness.why: a modifier on the primary score, worth at most 15% of that score. Readiness is real but conditional and remediable: a toolchain, a registry, and an observability stack can be fixed by process, while coupling written into the code cannot.

meta.label: Ecosystem coupling
meta.why: it is a dependency context, not a quality: a near-monoculture ecosystem lowers risk through consistency, so its band can disagree with its number. It is a lens, and it stays sortable, but it does not rank.

aggregation.rationale: Coupling is primary. A language that forces accidental coupling into every line has damaged the artifact permanently, and the artifact is what a maintainer faces for most of a system's life. Readiness surrounds the code rather than entering it, and it is remediable by process. So readiness does not weigh against coupling as a peer: it modifies the coupling score by at most the LIFT fraction — 15% of the language's own coupling score, which is 15 points only at a core of 100 and proportionally less below it. A language scoring 100 on readiness can therefore overtake at most a 15% coupling gap, and never a large one. The LIFT value is an authored choice, stated here beside the inventory, the mechanism weights, and the band thresholds; a reader who wants pure coupling sorts by that column.
